title: Yudhishthira's Final Trial
body:
Yudhishthira's Final Trial

When the news of Sree Krishna's passing reached Hastinapur, the Pandavas lost all remaining attachment to life on earth. Crowning Abhimanyu's son, Parikshit, as the next emperor, Yudhishthira, his four brothers, and Queen Draupadi set off on their final pilgrimage (Mahaprasthanam) toward the frozen heights of the Himalayas. Somewhere along the wearisome journey, a stray dog joined them and kept silent company.
As they climbed the steep, frozen slopes, one by one, they fell exhausted and died. First fell Draupadi, then Sahadeva, Nakula, Arjuna, and finally the mighty Bhima. At each fall, Yudhishthira explained their subtle attachments—Draupadi's partiality for Arjuna, Sahadeva's pride in learning, Nakula's vanity in physical beauty, Arjuna's boastful pride, and Bhima's gluttony. Serenely, Yudhishthira went on, never wavering, his mind anchored strictly in the Transcendent Truth. The dog alone followed him.
At the summit of the mountain, Lord Indra descended in a blazing golden chariot: 'Your wife and brothers have arrived in heaven before you. Ascend my chariot in your physical body and come with me.' But as Yudhishthira went to step into the chariot, the dog also climbed up. Indra pushed the dog back, saying, 'There is no place for dogs in heaven.'
Yudhishthira stopped, refusing to enter: 'This dog has followed me faithfully through the frozen wastes when all my brothers and wife have left me. To desert a devoted companion for the sake of my own happiness is a heinous sin. I shall not enter heaven without this dog.' At that instant, the dog transformed into Lord Dharma, who blessed his son for his peerless compassion.
Upon entering heaven, Yudhishthira was shocked to see Duryodhana seated in glory. His heart flamed with old anger, but Sage Narada corrected his vision: 'In swarga, we harbour no ill-will. Duryodhana has attained this state through his Kshatriya dharma. Discard your human prejudices.'
Yudhishthira demanded to see his brothers. A messenger led him down a dark, slippery path filled with the stench of blood, offal, and rotting flesh. Worms wriggled everywhere, and horrific sights of torture emerged from the gloom. As Yudhishthira turned back in disgust, familiar, agonising voices rose from the darkness: 'O Dharmaputra, stay here! Your pure presence brings a sweet breeze that mitigates our torture. Do not desert us!' Hearing the voices of Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, Sahadeva, and Draupadi, Yudhishthira was filled with rage and grief. He ordered the messenger: 'Go back to your masters! I shall remain here in hell with my suffering brothers rather than enjoy heaven alone!'
Immediately, the illusion of hell rolled away. Lord Dharma and Indra appeared, and the dark horrors dissolved into radiant light. Lord Dharma smiled upon his son: 'Wisest of men, this is the third time I have tested you. It is inevitable that kings must glimpse hell for a brief moment. Your brothers and Karna are already in radiant glory. Your choice to stay in hell for their sake was your final transfiguration.'
Yudhishthira bathed in the sacred, celestial Ganga, casting off his mortal frame and all physical memories of hatred, grief, and conflict. He entered the eternal, blemishless plane of supreme devotion—concluding the grand journey of the soul through the path of the Mahabharata.
